set.hook: A Nordic-trained tasting kitchen in a glass box on the fifth floor of the Greek National Opera.

set.hook: A Cappadocian-refugee deli and meze room by Varvakios market, built around pastourma and soutzouki.
set.why: The Karamanlides were Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians from Cappadocia who printed books in Turkish using the Greek alphabet, and many reached Greece in the 1923 exchange. Fanis Theodoropoulos, from a family of charcutiers on Evripidou, turned their cured-meat tradition into a deli with tables in 2014. One side is a counter of pastourma, soutzouki and cheeses; the other serves meze built from them. Vacuum-packed cuts travel well.

set.hook: The 1922 Armenian pastourma shop on Evripidou: cured beef by weight, with a small tasting corner.
set.why: In 1922 Miran Kourounlian, an Armenian refugee from Caesarea in Cappadocia, began curing beef into pastourma in Piraeus; a few years later he opened a narrow shop at Evripidou 45. A renovation gave the old counter a facade of living plants, and inside a tasting corner serves the house pastourma, soutzouki and cured beef in the middle of the spice street's trade.

set.hook: An Ano Petralona mageireio from 1930, opposite the Zefyros open-air cinema, where the day's pots run out.

set.hook: An Ilisia grill since 1967, up a short flight of steps: offal, chops and oven lamb for the hospital quarter.

set.hook: A small Voulis Street bistro pulling Greek produce through Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Chinese cooking.

set.hook: A Georgian tone-oven bakery in Kypseli: khachapuri, lavash and stuffed pies baked in front of you.
set.why: Marili is the Georgian word for salt, and Natia Nadareishvili chose it for the one thing a baker back home is never forgiven for getting wrong. She opened in 2023 with Londa Glonti and set a tone, the clay oven of the Caucasus, where customers can watch every pie go in. Athens Voice sent readers up to Kypseli for hot homemade khachapuri. The menu runs to lavash, piroshki and pouches of potato, bean or mushroom, the food of a quarter where Georgian is now heard on the street.

set.hook: Athens' last old-style galaktopoleio, off Omonia: sheep's-milk yogurt, honey and walnuts at a marble counter.
set.why: Nikolaos Karageorgos, a dairyman from Fokida, opened Stani in Piraeus in 1931, and after wartime bombing the family moved it to Marikas Kotopouli in 1949. In the 1960s Athens and Piraeus had some 1,600 of these milk shops; this is the one left, now run by his grandchildren. The yogurt is strained sheep's milk from small farms, served on a plate with honey and walnuts. In 1953 it took a gold award at the Thessaloniki International Fair. Order at the counter and pay as you go.
set.hours: Early morning to late evening; one listing gives 06:30-22:45 (undated) - call ahead

set.hook: A 1923 loukoumades house on Aiolou, in Athens' first pharmacy building: hot rings in honey and cinnamon.
set.why: The name on the front belongs to a pharmacist. In 1855 Stamatios Krinos, a professor at the Athens medical school, bought the Aiolou building and opened a pharmacy; in 1923 Minas Kasimatis, a refugee from Asia Minor, took it over for sweets and kept the name. The loukoumades are fried as rings with a hole in the middle, then soaked in honey and dusted with cinnamon. Mosaic floor and marble tables survive, and you order at the counter. Athinorama, in May 2026, still called them the city's most historic.

set.hook: A Thissio specialty-coffee house from Greece's competition baristas, with brunch in a neoclassical shell.
set.why: Co-founder Tasos Delichristos won the World Coffee in Good Spirits title in 2008, and he later coached Michalis Dimitrakopoulos to the same world championship in 2016. The beans are roasted daily at the company's own roastery in Gazi and brewed on three floors of a neoclassical house on Irakleidon, with an industrial-style courtyard at the back. Order the flat white or the cold brew first; reviewers split on whether the brunch matches the cup. Weekday mornings are the time to get a seat.

set.hook: A tiny souvlaki counter by Agia Irini church since 1946: pork, tomato and a red sauce in three strengths.
set.why: Kostas has wrapped souvlaki beside the church of Agia Eirini since 1946, and the counter is so small that the queue on the square is the dining room. The tomato is chopped for each pita, and the thin red sauce, sweet, medium or hot, is the house patent; regulars call the hot one 'the medicine'. Directories list it as Ta Souvlakia tou Kyr Kosta. Do not confuse it with the unrelated Kostas near Syntagma on Mitropoleos and Pentelis, which dates its tradition to 1950.
set.caveat: Standing room only, cash advised, and the shutter drops when the meat runs out. Expect a long queue in the sun at lunch. One LiFO piece says the shop moved into a side lane off the square after damage to its building, while directories still list Plateia Agias Eirinis 2 - look around the square if the old door is shut.

set.hook: The Cookoovaya chefs' souvlaki house on Agia Irini square: own butcher line, own bakery, pita from the oven.
set.why: In January 2018 five chefs from Cookoovaya, among them Nikos Karathanos and Periklis Koskinas, opened a souvlaki shop that does every job itself. set.hook: Monastiraki's kebab house since the 1960s: charcoal-grilled lamb-and-beef kebab on pita, open past 01:00.
set.why: Thanasis has stood at Mitropoleos 69, where the street opens onto Monastiraki square, since the mid-1960s, and across the road Bairaktaris has been its rival for just as long. set.hook: A family pie shop behind Parliament since the early 1900s, famous for its buttery half-moon tyropita kourou.
set.why: The founder carried the kourou recipe, a short buttery dough, from Constantinople, and the family has made it on Voulis Street ever since. After 1974, one Greek article reports, it sold up to ten thousand cheese pies a day; today it bakes well over a hundred kinds of pie daily. The sign says 'since 1910', but FNL Guide dates the founding to 1906 and reads 1910 as a nod to the street number. Buy, walk, eat.
set.caveat: Takeaway only, no tables and no coffee, and the trays empty early; reviewers note it closes early. Closed Sunday per the old record (not re-checked).

set.hook: The Psyrri bakery behind many of downtown's koulouri carts: sesame rings straight from the oven, day or night.
set.why: Ilias Papageorgiou, whom Greek press calls the pioneer of the koulouri, bought this Karaiskaki bakery in 1965, in a building from 1934. It became the source for the street carts that sell sesame rings on downtown corners, and the vendors still load up here before sunrise. Beside the classic ring you will find a thicker braided one made for sandwiches, cheese and sunflower-seed versions, and a sweet ring with currants and cinnamon. There are no seats; buy at the till and eat it warm.
set.hours: Listed as open around the clock (Tripadvisor; This is Athens calls it an all-night bakery) - hot rings are surest at dawn; call ahead to confirm
set.caveat: A production bakery with a till: no seats and no air conditioning, which a summer 2026 reviewer felt. Service is brisk.

set.hook: A Mets canteen below the Panathenaic Stadium: point at the day's trays of home cooking and sit down.
set.why: This is Athens describes the clientele in one line: undertakers, taxi drivers, students and pensioners, which makes sense on a lane between the Panathenaic Stadium and the First Cemetery. There is no printed menu. You walk to the kitchen, look at the trays and point: stuffed tomatoes, stews, courgettes in egg and lemon, giant beans from the oven. Zisimos Drakontaeidis has cooked here since the early 2000s, for years alongside his mother. Spring 2026 diners still rated the value highest of all.

set.hook: The last patsas kitchen in the Varvakios meat hall, since 1898: tripe soup and boiled goat at marble tables.
set.why: The house dates itself to 1898 and is the only patsatzidiko left inside the Varvakios meat market, with marble tables set among the butchers' hooks on the Filopoimenos side. In 2023 it was bought by Vasilis Akrivos, the cook behind Psariston in Neo Irakleio and Gidi in Metamorfosi, who calls it the Acropolis of Greek dining. He kept the patsas, white and with trotters, and the Easter mageiritsa that people queue for. Season it the market way: chilli flakes and garlic vinegar.

set.hook: A Thessaloniki-style bougatsa shop on Psyrri's Plateia Iroon, open through the night on weekends.
set.why: On Heroes' Square, at the Miaouli corner, the phyllo for bougatsa is stretched by hand on a marble slab in the window, the way the dawn bougatsa shops of Thessaloniki do it. The owner, Natasa, works from recipes her grandfather brought down from the north. Fill it with custard, minced meat or salty cheese; the custard one comes under cinnamon and icing sugar. The square fills with people leaving the bars, and on Friday and Saturday the shop does not close at all. Spinach pie is the second order.

set.hook: A former butcher's shop in Kerameikos turned late-night kalamaki counter: pork skewers, fries, no wraps.
set.why: The shop on the corner of Plataion and Leonidou was a butcher's before it was a souvlaki counter, and it kept the name Elvis from the days it served as a TV set. Spyros Athanasiou and Vangelis Petridis made it a place for one thing: pork or chicken skewers off the charcoal, a slice of grilled pita and hand-cut fries, with a yellow sauce they do not explain. Athinorama readers voted it first for kalamaki. It gets busiest after midnight, when the Kerameikos bars let out.
set.caveat: Not for wrap-seekers or anyone needing a proper table - a counter that peaks after midnight. A second Elvis near Plateia Plastira (Kallimarmaro) has its own Tripadvisor page; the guide means the Kerameikos original. Late hours not re-confirmed by a 2026 source.
